demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette:
Raj is a 52-year-old man who works as a maid at a mid-range hotel in a suburban city. He is of South Asian descent, divorced, and lives alone in a small apartment. The event that changed everything happened two years ago, when he was cleaning a hallway on the second floor. He was pushing a heavy cart loaded with linens and cleaning supplies when one of the wheels caught on a frayed carpet edge. The cart tipped suddenly, and a metal shelf bracket-meant to hold extra towels-swung out and struck an elderly guest who was walking past. She fell backward, hitting her head on the doorframe of her room. Raj remembers it as a sequence of frozen images: the wheel locking, the bracket swinging, the woman's eyes widening, the dull sound of skull against wood. The woman sustained a serious traumatic brain injury and spent months in rehabilitation. She survived, but with permanent cognitive deficits.

In the weeks and months after, Raj found that certain things could instantly bring the full memory back without any warning. The clatter of a dropped tray, the squeak of a cart wheel, the sight of an elderly guest walking slowly-each could transport him back to that hallway. When that happens, he sees the images again, and he feels a wave of intense rage. It is a hot, violent anger that surprises him, directed partly at himself for being careless and partly at the hotel for not fixing the carpet. But the rage never lasts; it quickly collapses into a hollow, sinking feeling. He has come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted-he should have checked the wheel, he should have slowed down, he should have seen her coming. Raj repeatedly tells himself that he acted in ways that go against who he is; he was raised to be careful, to never cause harm, and now that principle feels shattered. Nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. His work, once a source of modest pride, now feels like a stage where he might again fail someone else.

The memory of the accident directly feeds these negative appraisals. Each time a trigger throws him back into one of those snapshot moments, he is flooded not only with the visual image but with the accompanying rage, and from that rage he instantly pivots to self-blame and a sense of violated values-a loop that has tightened over the past two years. He has stopped taking breaks near the elevators because the sound of doors opening reminds him of the moment the guest stepped into the hallway. He drives a longer route home to avoid the street where the ambulance came. He has not visited his only son in three months, because his son's apartment is near the hospital where the woman was treated. These avoidances have drained his life of connection and variety, though they feel necessary to prevent the memories.

At work, the hotel management has been understanding, but his supervisors have noticed he no longer volunteers for extra shifts and sometimes freezes mid-task when a guest walks too close to his cart. Once, he nearly dropped a bucket of soapy water when an elderly woman asked him for directions, and he had to excuse himself to the supply closet until his hands stopped shaking. The rage on recall sometimes surfaces there, in that small room, and he has to press his palms against the wall to keep from hitting something.

Raj finally came to see a therapist because his ex-wife, with whom he still has occasional contact, told him that he looked "hollow." He was not sleeping, had lost weight, and had started drinking a few beers most evenings to dull the images. What frightens him most now is the feeling that the accident has erased any future he might have had. He is not suicidal, but he wonders what the point is of going on when he has proven to himself that he can harm another person without meaning to. He hopes, vaguely, that talking might help him feel less like a stranger to himself.
